title: Shah Rukh Khan-My-Ad
hook: A film star advertising your corner shop, made by a machine.
before: Lockdowns hit India’s small shops hard just before Diwali, Cadbury’s biggest season. In 2020 its ‘Not Just a Cadbury Ad’ had already promoted local businesses.
idea: Ogilvy Mumbai and Wavemaker used machine learning to let any small shop create a personalised ad in which Shah Rukh Khan named their business.
shift: Cadbury lent its biggest asset to thousands of local shops. The machine made a star’s endorsement affordable for the smallest business.
measure: Growth in the brand’s business reported in coverage of the campaign
evidence: The work won the 2023 Cannes Creative Effectiveness Grand Prix and topped WARC’s ranking of the most effective campaigns that year. The 35% growth comes from coverage of the entry, and the public record doesn’t show how it was modelled.
lesson: Use the machine to give people something they couldn’t get before.
test: The effectiveness entry reports business growth for the brand. The full method sits behind the awards records.
links: Watch Ogilvy’s case film and campaign executions
memorable: It flips the usual deal. The brand gave its celebrity away to the people who sell its chocolate.

creative.label: Watch the campaign film on Cadbury Celebrations’ channel

impact_source: Read the Grand Prix announcement · Ogilvy
metric_label: Business growth reported for the brand
take: My favourite AI idea anywhere. The machine didn’t replace anyone. It gave small shops a star they could never have afforded.
credit: Cannes Lions 2023 · Creative Effectiveness Grand Prix · Ogilvy Mumbai and Wavemaker for Mondelēz

image.alt: Shah Rukh Khan in a cream embroidered jacket in the Cadbury Celebrations ad
image.credit: Cadbury Celebrations and Ogilvy Mumbai, Shah Rukh Khan My Ad (2021) · Ogilvy

title: Deep Blue v Kasparov
hook: A computer beat the world chess champion, and a brand got the credit.
before: IBM’s Deep Blue had lost to Garry Kasparov in 1996. IBM Research sponsored a rematch in New York the following year.
idea: The six-game rematch was a public contest between a person and a machine, with IBM’s name on the machine.
shift: Deep Blue won 3½ to 2½. Kasparov accused IBM of cheating, which only added to the drama, and the match became the moment many people first saw a computer out-think a champion.
measure: The 1997 result. A milestone, not a marketing result
evidence: The record shows the match and its fame. No public source isolates what it did for IBM’s sales or reputation.
lesson: When the product is invisible, a contest can make it visible.
test: There is no effectiveness paper. The evidence is the historical record of the match.
links: Read IBM’s account of the Deep Blue rematch
memorable: It had a human face, an angry one. Kasparov’s reaction made the machine’s win feel real.

creative.label: Watch RTVE’s 1997 report on the rematch (Spanish)
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: The original AI stunt. It set the template every brand since has followed: put the machine against a person and let people watch.

image.alt: Garry Kasparov leaning over the chessboard during game four of the 1997 rematch
image.credit: Monroe Newborn, Kasparov during game four (1997) · Computer History Museum

title: Watson on Jeopardy!
hook: A quiz-show win that the business never quite matched.
before: IBM built Watson to answer questions in natural language, and chose the quiz show Jeopardy! as its public test.
idea: In 2011 Watson played Jeopardy! against human champions on television.
shift: Watson became IBM’s best-known product overnight. The business that followed struggled to live up to the show.
measure: The year Watson competed on Jeopardy!. A milestone, not a result
evidence: The win made Watson famous. Wikipedia reports that by 2023 Watson had cost IBM far more than it earned. Fame and commercial success came apart.
lesson: A great demonstration creates expectations. The product has to meet them afterwards.
test: There is no effectiveness paper. The record is the broadcast and what happened to Watson as a business.
links: Read IBM’s account of the televised competition
memorable: It made a machine look quick and clever in the most familiar format there is, a quiz.

creative.label: Watch ‘Watson and the Jeopardy! Challenge’ on IBM Research’s channel

take: The most honest warning in this edition. A machine that wins on stage still has to work in the office.

image.alt: Watson’s screen between the two human contestants at their Jeopardy! podiums
image.credit: IBM Research, Watson and the Jeopardy! Challenge · official film thumbnail

title: The Next Rembrandt
hook: A new Rembrandt, painted by a computer.
before: ING sponsored Dutch art and culture and wanted to show that technology could create as well as calculate.
idea: J. Walter Thompson Amsterdam worked with Microsoft and others to analyse Rembrandt’s paintings with data and machine learning, then 3D printed a new portrait in his style.
shift: A bank became the name behind one of the most talked-about tech stories of the year.
measure: Global media impressions reported by the agency, with no paid media
evidence: The agency reports 1.8bn impressions and two Cannes Grand Prix. These are self-reported reach figures. No public source links the project to ING’s customers or business.
lesson: If the machine makes something people can stand in front of, the story travels by itself.
test: The record is earned media and awards, reported by the agency.
memorable: It is a painting you can walk up to. The physical object makes the machine’s work feel real.

creative.label: Watch ‘The Next Rembrandt’ on the project’s channel

metric_label: Media impressions, with no paid media
take: Beautiful and much copied. I’d still like to know whether anyone opened an account because of it.
credit: Cannes Lions 2016 · Two Grand Prix · J. Walter Thompson Amsterdam for ING

image.alt: The project’s finished portrait of a man wearing a broad black hat and white collar
image.credit: ING and J. Walter Thompson Amsterdam, The Next Rembrandt (2016) · Güney Soykan’s project portfolio

title: Messi Messages
hook: A personal video message from Messi, for anyone who asked.
before: Lay’s sponsored the UEFA Champions League and wanted fans to feel close to its star, Lionel Messi.
idea: With Synthesia, Lay’s recorded Messi briefly in a studio, then let fans generate a video of him speaking to a friend by name, in several languages.
shift: A celebrity endorsement became a personal message, made on demand.
measure: Up to ten languages, per Marketing Dive. A scale fact, not a result
evidence: The campaign won a Cannes Lion. Its makers describe huge global shareability, but no public figure shows its effect on sales or the brand.
lesson: AI can scale intimacy. Whether that sells crisps still needs measuring.
test: There is no published effectiveness record, only award entries and the makers’ own descriptions.
links: Watch Synthesia explain how the Messi videos were made
memorable: Hearing a famous voice say your friend’s name is a strange, small thrill.

creative.label: Watch the 2021 Messi Messages spot on Lay’s Football

impact_source: Read the launch story · Marketing Dive
take: The friendliest use of a synthetic face in this edition. It worked because Messi agreed to it and fans controlled it.

image.alt: A phone showing Messi Messages on a yellow Lay’s campaign end card
image.credit: Lay’s, Messi Messages (2021) · still from Lay’s Football

title: A.I. Ketchup
hook: Ask a machine to draw ketchup, and it draws Heinz.
before: Heinz was so established it was synonymous with ketchup, but younger audiences didn’t see it as a contemporary brand.
idea: Rethink asked DALL-E 2 to show what ‘ketchup’ looked like. Most results looked like Heinz, so the brand invited people to suggest prompts and turned the images into ads, galleries and special bottles.
shift: The machine became an independent witness to the brand’s fame.
measure: Earned impressions after the campaign went global, per WARC
evidence: WARC reports more than 1.15bn earned impressions. That shows how far the joke travelled, not what it did for sales or for younger buyers.
lesson: If the machine’s answer flatters you, let it speak for you.
test: The record counts earned impressions and coverage.
memorable: It is a brag disguised as an experiment. Heinz didn’t say it was the only ketchup. The machine did.

creative.label: Watch A.I. Ketchup on Heinz’s channel

take: The smartest use of AI as a witness. It cost almost nothing and proved a point no ad could prove about itself.

image.alt: AI-generated red ketchup bottle above clouds against a blue outer-space background
image.credit: Heinz and Rethink, A.I. Ketchup (2022) · Xavier Blais’s creative portfolio

title: Create Real Magic
hook: Coca-Cola handed its brand assets to the public, with AI tools.
before: Generative AI was everywhere, and many in tech were calling for a pause. Coca-Cola wanted younger audiences to make something with its brand.
idea: Coca-Cola launched a platform that let creators use DALL-E and GPT with its iconic imagery. The best work appeared on billboards in Times Square and Piccadilly Circus.
shift: The brand’s look became something people could play with rather than just watch.
measure: Unique images created, with 316m media impressions and 90% positive sentiment, per WARC
evidence: The case reports over 120,000 images, more than 316m media impressions and 90% positive sentiment. These are reach and sentiment measures, not sales.
lesson: Give people the tools and the stage, and they will make the brand theirs.
test: The case counts images, impressions, posts and sentiment.
links: Read Coca-Cola’s announcement for the creative platform
memorable: Seeing your own picture on a billboard in Piccadilly Circus is a reward no discount can match.

creative.label: Watch the Create Real Magic launch film on Coca-Cola’s channel

take: Put this next to the Christmas remake a year later. Same company, same tools. Here people did the making, and they loved it.
data_source: DALL-E and GPT, used by the public

image.alt: The red Create Real Magic interface next to an artwork with a glass Coke bottle
image.credit: Coca-Cola, Create Real Magic (2023) · official launch film thumbnail

title: Never Done Evolving
hook: Serena Williams of 1999 plays Serena Williams of 2017.
before: Nike was marking its 50th anniversary and wanted to show what its athletes stand for: constant improvement.
idea: AKQA trained machine-learning models on Serena Williams’ play at the 1999 US Open and the 2017 Australian Open, then simulated a match between the two.
shift: An athlete’s career became a contest with herself, made possible by the machine.
measure: The two championships the models were built on. A creative fact, not a result
evidence: The work won the Digital Craft Grand Prix at Cannes in 2023. No public figure shows its effect on sales or the brand.
lesson: Use the machine to show something true about a person that couldn’t be filmed.
test: There is no published effectiveness record, only awards.
memorable: It answers a question every sports fan has asked, which version of a champion was best.

creative.label: Watch Never Done Evolving on AKQA’s Vimeo channel

take: The most respectful AI film here. It celebrates the athlete instead of replacing her.
credit: Cannes Lions 2023 · Digital Craft Grand Prix · AKQA for Nike

image.alt: Two versions of Serena Williams facing each other in Nike’s Never Done Evolving artwork
image.credit: Nike and AKQA, Never Done Evolving · agency campaign artwork

title: Cats Lose Their Cool
medium: Online video, social, print and TV
hook: An algorithm studied cat owners, and the ads made cats lose their cool.
before: Temptations, Dreamies in the UK, dominated cat treats so completely that more advertising brought diminishing returns. Mars chose it for its biggest US pet-food launch in a decade.
idea: adam&eveDDB’s ‘Cats Lose Their Cool’ was inspired by an algorithm that analysed how people talk about cats, and by a database of ‘perfect cat’ clichés from pop culture.
shift: The machine found the insight, and people made the jokes. Effortlessly cool cats lose all composure for a treat.
measure: Profit return estimated by econometrics, with $75m of sales, per the IPA case
evidence: Econometrics estimate $75m of sales and $1.54 of profit for every $1 invested. The algorithm shaped the creative, so the model measures the advertising as a whole rather than the machine’s part in it.
lesson: Let the machine listen, and let people write.
test: An econometric model estimated the sales and profit the advertising added during the launch.
memorable: Every cat owner knows the moment a cool cat hears the treat packet. The ads live in that moment.

creative.label: Watch the Artist spot at adam&eve

take: This is how I’d want AI in a creative department. It did the listening, and it never appeared in the ad.
data_source: An algorithm reading how people talk about cats

image.alt: A black-and-white cat wearing a patterned outfit and sitting on a stool
image.credit: Mars and adam&eveDDB, Cats Lose Their Cool (2023) · still from the agency’s Artist spot

title: Courage to Be Real
hook: A luxury brand that tested its way to Gen Z.
before: Coach wanted to win over Gen Z shoppers for whom an older handbag brand wasn’t an obvious choice.
idea: From 2023 Coach pre-tested its creative at every stage of production with Human Made Machine, then used the results to shape its storytelling and steer global media spend, with YouTube as the lead channel.
shift: Testing moved from a final check to part of how the work was made.
measure: Growth in Gen Z spending in early 2026, alongside a record $2.14bn quarter, per the IPA case
evidence: By 2025 Coach had increased its lead as Gen Z’s preferred handbag brand, and in early 2026 it reported a record $2.14bn quarter with Gen Z spending up 46%. These are business trends, not a modelled estimate of the advertising or the testing.
lesson: Test early and often, then let the results move the money.
test: The case links the pre-testing programme to brand preference and sales trends among Gen Z.
memorable: The films are about courage and self-expression, which is a nice irony for work shaped by so much testing.

creative.label: Watch Coach’s 2024 Find Your Courage recap on YouTube
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: Gen Z spending, year on year
take: The machine here is a stopwatch, not a director. It told people which version worked, and people made it.
credit: IPA 2026 · Human Made Machine for Coach

image.alt: Virtual model imma with pink hair on a rooftop in Find Your Courage
image.credit: Coach, Find Your Courage (2024) · official recap thumbnail

title: Holidays Are Coming, Remade
hook: The ad that tested brilliantly and still upset people.
before: ‘Holidays Are Coming’ is one of Coca-Cola’s best-loved Christmas films, built on nostalgia for the trucks and the lights.
idea: In 2024 Coca-Cola remade it with generative AI. Its marketing lead described the brief as bringing ‘Holidays Are Coming’ into the present, with AI as the solution.
shift: The brand got attention, but for the wrong reason. Viewers online called the film uncanny and soulless, and the debate was about the tool, not the holidays.
measure: System1’s top score in both the US and UK, reported before the backlash grew
evidence: System1’s testing found an overwhelmingly positive response, and its panel didn’t notice the film was made with AI. The public reaction online turned negative anyway. The two measures disagree, and neither shows the effect on sales.
lesson: A pre-test measures the ad. It doesn’t measure how people feel once they know how it was made.
test: Pre-launch testing scored the emotional response to the film. The backlash shows up only in social reaction and press coverage.
links: Read how the reaction turned · Adweek
See the other 2024 holiday films in Coca-Cola’s announcement
memorable: It is a remake of a memory. That makes any strangeness in the pictures easy to spot and hard to forgive.

creative.label: Watch Silver Santa, one of the 2024 AI holiday films, on Coca-Cola’s channel

take: This is the case for anyone who thinks testing settles the argument. It told Coca-Cola people liked the film, and it couldn’t tell them people would mind how it was made.

image.alt: A red Coca-Cola truck lit with Christmas lights in a snowy town
image.credit: Coca-Cola, Silver Santa (2024) · official film thumbnail

title: The Origin of Toys “R” Us
hook: A brand film made almost entirely by a video model.
before: Toys “R” Us had closed its US stores in 2018 and was rebuilding the brand.
idea: Native Foreign used OpenAI’s Sora to make a short film about the founder’s childhood, almost entirely generated with some corrective effects and an original score. It premiered at Cannes Lions in 2024.
shift: The conversation was about the tool. Critics called the film lifeless and worried about AI replacing creative work, while the company called it a successful test.
measure: One of the first brand films made almost entirely with Sora. A creative fact, not a result
evidence: The public record is reaction and coverage, much of it negative. The company called the film a success, but published no figures.
lesson: Being first with a tool is a story about the tool. Make sure that’s the story you want.
test: There is no published effectiveness record.
memorable: It looks like a dream of an advert, which is both its achievement and its problem.

creative.label: Watch the Sora-made origin film at Toys “R” Us Studios

take: A brave test, and a useful one for everyone else. It showed how quickly people notice what’s missing.
credit: Cannes Lions 2024 premiere · Native Foreign for Toys “R” Us

image.alt: Young Charles in glasses looking up as lights swirl around him
image.credit: Toys “R” Us Studios and Native Foreign, The Origin of Toys “R” Us (2024) · still from the brand film

title: The Code
hook: A beauty brand that promised never to use AI to show real women.
before: Twenty years after the Campaign for Real Beauty began, AI image tools were producing a narrow, unrealistic idea of beauty.
idea: In ‘The Code’ women type prompts into AI image generators and get impossible results. Dove pledged never to use AI to represent real women in its ads and published a prompt playbook for more realistic images.
shift: Dove made its position on AI part of what the brand stands for.
measure: Positive sentiment reported in an award entry, alongside 2m YouTube views
evidence: The award entry reports 94% positive sentiment and the biggest press coverage in Dove’s history. These are self-reported reach and sentiment figures.
lesson: Sometimes the most powerful thing a brand can say about a technology is what it won’t do.
test: The record counts views, sentiment and coverage.
memorable: The prompts are ordinary. The pictures they produce are not, and that gap is the whole argument.

creative.label: Watch ‘The Code’ on Dove UK’s channel

impact_source: Read the pledge announcement · PR Newswire
take: The neatest turn in the series. Dove, star of Edition 01, used AI as the villain to restate what it has always stood for.
data_source: AI image generators, used as the problem

image.alt: Two people with curly hair standing together in a still from The Code
image.credit: Dove, The Code (2024) · Dove’s Keep Beauty Real campaign page

title: A Creative System
hook: An airline that built its advertising for the algorithm first.
before: Holiday booking had changed and media had fragmented into algorithm-driven feeds. Traditional campaigns had become a straitjacket for easyJet.
idea: VCCP and partners built a system that combined media, creative and production, made assets for small behaviour-driving spaces first, and scaled what worked, using hand-picked creators and a content engine.
shift: The campaign became a system that keeps learning, and the algorithm decided where the work went.
measure: Incremental profit estimated by modelling, up 60% on the year before, per the IPA case
evidence: Modelling estimates £136m of incremental profit in 2025, up 60% year on year, and a 49% rise in margin ROI against a 10% target. It is one of the strongest results in this edition, and it comes from the machine working behind the scenes.
lesson: Build for the feed first, then scale what the feed tells you works.
test: Modelling estimated the incremental profit the system delivered and compared margin ROI with the target set for it.
links: See how VCCP built the Big Orange Sale campaign
memorable: There is no single ad to remember, and that is the point.

creative.label: Watch Big Orange Sale, a 2025 example of the system, on VCCP’s Vimeo
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: This is where the money is. The least glamorous use of machines in the edition has the biggest proven return.
credit: IPA 2026 · Bronze · VCCP, T&P and Kepler for easyJet
data_source: Algorithmic media and a content engine

image.alt: A woman with sunglasses holding a bright red fan in a sunny street
image.credit: easyJet and VCCP, Big Orange Sale (2025) · agency campaign artwork

title: The AI Christmas Ad
hook: A Christmas ad pulled after about three days.
before: A year after Coca-Cola’s AI Christmas film, McDonald’s Netherlands made its own festive ad about the stress of the holidays.
idea: The 45-second film used generative AI. It went up on the brand’s Dutch YouTube channel in December 2025.
shift: Viewers called it creepy and cynical, and McDonald’s took it down within days, calling the episode an important learning. The production company defended the craft behind it.
measure: About three days online before it was withdrawn. A fact, not a result
evidence: The record is the backlash and the withdrawal. There are no published figures on effect.
lesson: When a format is built on warmth, the audience will judge the method as much as the message.
test: There is no effectiveness record. The evidence is the reaction and the company’s decision.
memorable: It tried to be honest about Christmas stress, and the method drowned out the message.

creative.label: Watch an archived reupload of the withdrawn 2025 Christmas advert
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: Roughly how long it stayed online
take: Coca-Cola went first and took the hit. McDonald’s went second and still didn’t see it coming. That’s the lesson of this whole edition.

image.alt: A choir of Santas beneath the McDonald’s arches in a snowy street
image.credit: McDonald’s Netherlands, TBWA\Neboko and The Sweetshop, 2025 Christmas spot · still published by Adformatie
